name: Davunetide
evidenceNote: Davunetide reached randomized, placebo-controlled human trials, including a 313-patient phase 2/3 study, so the evidence base is real. That pivotal trial was clearly negative, and the smaller positive signals in other conditions were never confirmed.
summary: Davunetide is an eight-amino-acid nasal spray peptide tested for brain diseases. Its main trial in progressive supranuclear palsy failed.
keyTakeaway: Davunetide, also called NAP, is an eight-amino-acid peptide taken from a brain-protecting protein called ADNP and given as a nasal spray. Lab studies suggested it steadies microtubules (the tubes that give nerve cells their shape) and limits harmful changes to the tau protein. Allon Therapeutics took it into human trials, but its largest study, a 313-patient phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy, found no difference from placebo on either main measure after a year. Small earlier trials in memory decline and schizophrenia were never confirmed. It is not FDA-approved, and no trials are currently recruiting.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Proposed to stabilize nerve-cell microtubules and reduce abnormal tau changes, based on lab and animal work

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Pivotal phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy was negative on both primary endpoints

blocks.text: Davunetide is a short peptide with the sequence NAPVSIPQ, eight amino acids long, and the lab name NAP comes from its first three letters [1]. It is a fragment of activity-dependent neuroprotective protein (ADNP), a protein the developing brain needs to form properly and that helps control hundreds of genes [1].

The company Allon Therapeutics developed it as a nasal spray under the codes AL-108 and AL-208, aiming at diseases where nerve cells lose their structure, especially those driven by the tau protein [2][4]. It was tested in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare movement and thinking disorder caused by tau buildup, and earlier in mild memory decline and schizophrenia [1][3].

Nerve cells rely on microtubules, long hollow tubes that give them shape and carry cargo along their length. The protein tau normally helps hold microtubules together. In tau diseases, tau becomes overloaded with phosphate groups, detaches, and clumps into tangles, leaving microtubules exposed.

Much of the case for davunetide came from mice. Animals with only half the normal amount of ADNP developed memory problems and tau changes, and giving NAP partly reversed those changes [1]. That made the peptide look like a way to replace a missing protective signal. The leap from a genetically altered mouse to a person with a decades-long brain disease is large, and this is where many brain drugs falter.

In cell and animal studies, davunetide protected microtubules from being cut apart when tau levels were low, and it reduced the death of nerve cells through survival signaling pathways [1]. In preclinical work it also lowered tau phosphorylation, which was the rationale for testing it in PSP [2]. These findings describe what happened in laboratory models. As the trials below show, they did not carry over into measurable benefit in patients.

No. Davunetide has never been approved for any condition by the FDA or any other major regulator. After its phase 2/3 trial in PSP failed, the lead program stopped. The ClinicalTrials.gov registry lists the PSP study and its earlier trials as completed, with none recruiting [4].
It is not sold as a medicine. Any product marketed online as NAP or davunetide has not been reviewed for safety, purity, or effect.

items.text: Allon begins trials in mild cognitive impairment; a university group starts a schizophrenia study [4].
Phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy starts across six countries [2][4].
Schizophrenia trial reports no effect on its main cognitive measure [3].
PSP results published: no benefit over placebo [2].

blocks.text: The deciding study was a randomized, double-blind trial at 48 centers in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the UK, and the US. It enrolled 313 people with PSP, who used davunetide spray twice daily or a placebo for 52 weeks [2]. The two primary measures were a PSP rating scale and a scale of everyday independence. On both, the groups changed by the same amount, and the investigators judged the drug ineffective for PSP [2].

rows: No difference from placebo on either primary endpoint [2]
63 people with schizophrenia on their usual medicines
No effect on the main cognitive battery; one functional skills test favored the drug [3]
Improved memory scores reported in early studies, not confirmed in larger trials [1]

blocks.text: Safety in the PSP trial was broadly similar between groups, with 54 serious adverse events in each arm, including 11 deaths on davunetide and 10 on placebo. Nose problems were more common on the drug: nosebleeds in 12% vs 8%, runny nose in 10% vs 5%, and nasal discomfort in 10% vs under 1% [2].

The schizophrenia study was small. Davunetide did not beat placebo on the MATRICS cognitive battery, its main measure, though a test of everyday functional skills reached significance across the groups [3]. The memory-decline results come from the developer's side and were never followed by a confirmatory trial [1]. Taken together, the human evidence does not show that davunetide helps any condition it was tested in.

sections.heading: What did the failed trial leave behind?

blocks.text: The PSP trial still mattered. It showed that a year-long, placebo-controlled study in a rare and fast-moving disease can be run across dozens of sites in six countries. The investigators argued that other tau-targeting drugs should be tested the same way [2].

For davunetide itself, the result means the lab rationale did not hold up in people with established disease. Earlier positive hints in memory decline and schizophrenia came from small or developer-linked studies and were never tested in a larger trial [1][3]. Without new randomized evidence, claims that the peptide protects the brain rest on animal work alone.
